+[Figure 2, p. 3](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-2) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form.

+Panel B shows the exponential-transfer simulation with 1,024 neurons. Its inset compares activity patterns 10 seconds apart. The horizontal axis orders neurons around the ring; the solid curves show their firing rates, with peaks near 85 Hz. Vertical marks show the spikes emitted in a 10 ms window at each snapshot. The peak moves between snapshots. The main trace follows the represented angle through time, rather than overall activity amplitude. [The pattern can persist while its position, and therefore the remembered value, changes.]{.key-statement}
**Interpretation of the simulation tests.** Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction:

-- Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula.

+- Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions, shown in its inset. Circles are simulation measurements; solid lines are the diffusion prediction from Eq. 2. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. Error bars in C and D show [the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: uncertainty in the mean MSD estimated from 100 trials, rather than the spread of individual trial values.]{.definition-explanation} In C they are smaller than the symbols.
-- Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals. Its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$.

+- Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals. Its theoretical curve inserts the predicted diffusion coefficient into the wrapped-angle mean squared error formula, SI Eq. S32. It therefore includes the effect of periodic boundaries rather than extending the short-lag straight line indefinitely. Its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$.

-Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions. Their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]

+Panel E replaces the ring with two mutually inhibiting units, which can also represent two neural populations. Equal opposing weights and a linear firing rule support a continuous range of rate differences. That difference represents a nonperiodic stored value, rather than an angle that wraps around.

+In F the two rates vary in opposite directions. The vertical axis uses $\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$: one spike per millisecond is 1,000 spikes per second. The large plotted rates can describe the summed activity of each population. They should not be read as ordinary rates of two individual biological neurons.

+Panel G asks how far their rate difference changes over a lag. For each lag, the authors square that change and average over starting times in the 200-second simulation. Its vertical axis therefore has units $(\mathrm{ms}^{-1})^2$, while its horizontal axis is lag in seconds. Circles are those measurements; the solid line is the diffusion prediction from Eq. 2. The [simulation chapter](ch-simulating-memory.html#sec-simulating-memory-controls) writes out the measured quantity and its unit conversion. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]

Converting between activation and rate changes the units of the stored value. Let $\theta_s=s_1-s_2$ be the activation difference and $\theta_r=r_1-r_2$ the rate difference along the steady-state family. Since $s_i=\tau r_i$ there, $\theta_r=\theta_s/\tau$ and their diffusion coefficients satisfy $D_r=D_s/\tau^2$. Their units differ, so their numerical values should not be compared without this conversion. A population can also emit several spikes within one update. The ring's at-most-one-spike rule cannot be copied into this setting. The paper specifies a Poisson process but does not say how spike counts were drawn or give the complete initial state for this example.

+To reproduce Figure 2G, the measured displacement must be a change in the rate difference, not a change in either rate alone. Write $T=200\,\mathrm{s}$ for the recording duration and $\ell$ for the lag. Using the rate coordinate $\theta_r(t)=r_1(t)-r_2(t)$, the plotted statistic is

+The hat marks an average calculated from the finite simulation. For each lag, take both rates at the beginning and end of every available interval, form their differences, square the change, and average those squared changes over starting times. At a 2-second lag, for example, valid starts run from 0 to 198 seconds. Intervals can overlap, so these are not independent trials. The average uses many positions along one simulated trajectory; it is not the 100-trial standard error calculation used for the ring panels.

+Figure 2F reports rates in $\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$, so G reports squared rate displacements in $(\mathrm{ms}^{-1})^2$. If a reproduction stores rates in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, divide its squared displacements by $10^6$ to compare their numerical values with G. The theoretical line must use $2D_r\ell$ in the same units. [Agreement tests whether the predicted diffusion gives the spreading of the simulated rate difference.]{.key-statement} It does not compare the rate trace with a recorded animal's memory errors.[^simmem-two]

The supporting text also tests a mutually excitatory pair in Figure S1. Across 4,000 trials started at the same coordinate, its variance grows linearly even though the local diffusion coefficient depends on the state. The guide's [long-delay chapter](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) explains the coordinate and the printed factor-of-two discrepancy. That discrepancy is separate from the authors' 2017 correction.
## A plotted analytical curve is different from a network simulation {#sec:SIMULATING-MEMORY-OUTPUTS}

-Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell's reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Pearson correlation is the ordinary linear correlation defined as $\rho$ in the [foundations](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-covariance); this paper writes it as $R$. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was $\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02$, [where the error is the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals.]{.definition-explanation} The one sided test gave $p=3.8\times10^{-12}$. Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation]
